$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{100}{\sqrt{1-10{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =100\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{10}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =100\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{100}{\sqrt{10}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{100\sqrt{10}}{10}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =10\sqrt{10}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{64-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{64\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/64)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/64}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/8)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{8})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{8}.$ Differentiating, we get  

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=8\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
